beforeRecord.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
beforeRecord.q: An economy initially has 90 employed and 10 unemployed adults out of 150. Five unemployed people stop searching, and no one finds a job. How do unemployment and participation change, and what employment conclusion follows?
options: Unemployment 5.3%, participation 63.3%; exit lowered the rate without creating jobs.
Unemployment 5%, participation 66.7%; five people found jobs.
Unemployment 10%, participation 60%; search does not affect unemployment.
Unemployment 10.5%, participation 70%; exit raises both denominators.
beforeRecord.feedback: Employment stays 90, unemployment falls to 5, and the labor force becomes 95. The new unemployment rate is 5/95 ≈ 5.3%, while participation is 95/150 ≈ 63.3%, down from 66.7%. Neither change records an employment gain; the lower unemployment rate alone misses the discouraged exit.

afterRecord.commonError: Incorrect inference: The unemployment rate falls; employment rises to 95.
afterRecord.q: Initially, 90 adults are employed and 10 are unemployed. Five unemployed adults stop searching for work. What happens to the unemployment rate and the number employed?
options: The unemployment rate falls; employment stays at 90.
The unemployment rate falls; employment rises to 95.
The unemployment rate rises; employment stays at 90.
The unemployment rate stays unchanged; employment falls to 85.
afterRecord.feedback: People who stop searching leave both unemployment and the labor force. The unemployment rate falls from 10 ÷ 100 = 10% to 5 ÷ 95, about 5.3%. No one found a job, so employment remains 90.

changes.reason: Keep the labor-market application while removing unnecessary precision and repeated ratio calculations.

beforeRecord.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
beforeRecord.q: The adult population is 250 million, participation is 64%, and unemployment is 8 million. Later, 4 million unemployed people find jobs and 4 million employed people retire and leave the labor force. What happens to employment, unemployment, and participation?
options: Employment stays at 152 million, unemployment falls to 4 million, and participation falls to 62.4%.
Employment rises to 156 million, unemployment falls to 4 million, and participation stays at 64%.
Employment stays at 152 million, unemployment stays at 8 million, and participation stays at 64%.
Employment falls to 148 million, unemployment falls to 4 million, and participation falls to 60.8%.
beforeRecord.feedback: Initially the labor force is 0.64 × 250 = 160 million and employment is 160 − 8 = 152 million. Job finding adds 4 million to employment while retirement subtracts 4 million, leaving employment unchanged. Unemployment becomes 4 million and the labor force 156 million, so participation is 156/250 = 62.4%.

afterRecord.commonError: Incorrect inference: Employment rises to 156; participation stays at 64%.
afterRecord.q: Of 250 adults, 152 are employed and 8 are unemployed. Four unemployed adults find jobs while four employed adults retire and leave the labor force. What happens to employment and labor-force participation?
options: Employment stays at 152; participation falls from 64% to 62.4%.
Employment rises to 156; participation stays at 64%.
Employment stays at 152; participation stays at 64%.
Employment falls to 148; participation falls to 60.8%.
afterRecord.feedback: The four new hires offset the four retirements, so employment stays at 152. The labor force falls from 160 to 156 because the retirees leave it. With 250 adults, participation falls from 160 ÷ 250 = 64% to 156 ÷ 250 = 62.4%.

changes.reason: Keep the labor-market application while removing unnecessary precision and repeated ratio calculations.

beforeRecord.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
beforeRecord.q: A population of 200 adults is unchanged. The unemployment rate stays at 6%, while participation falls from 75% to 70%. Which employment change and interpretation follow?
options: Employment falls by 9.4 despite the unchanged unemployment rate
Employment stays at 141; a stable rate fixes employment
Employment falls by 10; every labor-force exit must be an employed worker
Employment rises by 9.4; lower participation indicates more jobs
beforeRecord.feedback: The labor force falls from 150 to 140. Employment is 94% of each total: 141 initially and 131.6 afterward, a decline of 9.4. The unchanged unemployment rate is a ratio, not an unchanged employment count.

afterRecord.commonError: Incorrect inference: Yes; an unchanged unemployment rate guarantees unchanged employment.
afterRecord.q: A population stays at 1,000 adults. Labor-force participation falls from 60% to 50%, while the unemployment rate remains 10%. A report says the unchanged unemployment rate means employment was stable. Is that correct?
options: No; employment falls by 90 because fewer adults participate.
Yes; an unchanged unemployment rate guarantees unchanged employment.
No; employment rises by 90 because fewer people seek work.
Yes; participation excludes employed adults.
afterRecord.feedback: Initially, 600 adults participate and 90% of them are employed: 540. Later, 500 participate and 450 are employed. Employment falls by 90 despite an unchanged unemployment rate. Reading the rate alongside participation reveals the change.

beforeRecord.q: Automation raises output per worker and lowers production costs, but some workers in the old process lose jobs and need retraining. Which statement best describes the combined effect?
options: Productivity must fall when workers are displaced, even if output per worker rises and unit costs fall
Productivity can rise while displaced workers face only frictional search, even when their old skills no longer fit vacancies
Productivity and potential living standards can rise while displaced workers face a structural skill mismatch requiring adjustment
Productivity can rise while displaced workers face only cyclical unemployment that disappears as soon as the new machines operate
beforeRecord.feedback: Technology can raise productivity and living standards over time while displacing some workers whose skills no longer match the market.

afterRecord.q: Automation raises output per worker and lowers production costs, but some workers in the old process lose jobs and need retraining. Which statement best describes the combined effect?
options: Productivity must fall when workers are displaced, even if output per worker rises and unit costs fall
Productivity can rise while displaced workers face only frictional search, even when their old skills no longer fit vacancies
Productivity and potential living standards can rise while displaced workers face a structural skill mismatch requiring adjustment
Productivity can rise while displaced workers face only cyclical unemployment that disappears as soon as the new machines operate
afterRecord.commonError: treats_growth_and_displacement_as_mutually_exclusive
afterRecord.feedback: Automation raises output per worker and lowers unit costs, expanding potential living standards. Workers whose skills no longer fit available jobs may still face structural unemployment during the adjustment. Higher productivity and transitional hardship can occur together; retraining can help workers share in the gains.

changes.reason: Explain the productivity-displacement synthesis in full natural prose.

beforeRecord.q: Demand is at its normal level. Each week, 40 qualified workers start searching for suitable existing vacancies. Average search lasts 6 weeks. A job-information service cuts that duration to 3 weeks without changing entries into search or job requirements. Another 180 job seekers lack the skills vacancies require. Assume steady flows, so the frictionally unemployed equal weekly entries times average search duration. What does the service change, and what would address the remaining mismatch?
options: Frictional unemployment falls by 240; retraining addresses the 180 mismatched workers, while demand stimulus alone need not do so.
Frictional unemployment falls by 120; the information service also removes all structural unemployment without retraining.
Frictional unemployment falls by 120; retraining addresses the 180 mismatched workers, while demand stimulus alone need not do so.
Frictional unemployment stays unchanged; only stronger aggregate demand can shorten search when suitable vacancies already exist.
beforeRecord.commonError: Confusing shorter search spells with fewer entrants or with elimination of a skill mismatch.
beforeRecord.feedback: The steady search stock falls from 40×6=240 to 40×3=120. Better information reduces search time and frictional unemployment. It does not supply missing skills, so the separate structural mismatch calls for a skill response. At normal demand, an aggregate-demand increase is not a substitute for these targeted changes.

afterRecord.q: A job-information service reduces the number of qualified workers searching for suitable vacancies from 240 to 120. Another 180 job seekers still lack the skills employers require. Demand is at its normal level. How should the program’s success and the remaining policy need be assessed?
options: Structural unemployment falls by 120; more job listings alone will qualify the remaining workers.
Cyclical unemployment falls by 120; further demand stimulus will supply the missing skills.
Frictional unemployment falls by 120; retraining addresses the separate skills mismatch.
The program failed because 180 workers still lack the skills required for vacancies.
afterRecord.commonError: Incorrect inference: Structural unemployment falls by 120; more job listings alone will qualify the remaining workers.
afterRecord.feedback: Faster matching reduces unemployment among qualified applicants, a frictional improvement. It does not provide the skills that the other group lacks. At normal demand, relevant training addresses that structural barrier more directly than additional demand stimulus. A program can succeed on one problem while a different problem remains.
